activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine works by fitting into nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, proteins on brain cells that normally respond to the brain's own chemical messenger, acetylcholine.
story:
The science fair was eleven days away, and Emile still could not explain the thing on his poster. The heading said "How Nicotine Hooks the Brain," and under it he had taped a diagram of a brain cell with a sad face drawn on it. That was not science. That was a sad face.

He cornered his partner Giuliano in the library after last period. Giuliano had a laptop open to a medical database, scrolling so fast the screen blurred.

"Look," Giuliano said, turning the screen. "Receptors. They're proteins on brain cells." He tapped a diagram. "The brain has its own chemical messenger, called acetylcholine. It fits into these receptors like a key in a lock."

"So the messenger is the key," Emile said slowly.

"And nicotine is a fake key. Same shape, fits the same lock." Giuliano spun the laptop toward him. "Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. That's what they're called, because nicotine fits them too."

Emile sat down so fast the chair squeaked. A fake key. He could see the whole poster suddenly: a door, a real key, a copy of the key, and a brain cell on the other side. He grabbed his notebook and started sketching before the idea could leak away.

Then the problem arrived. Ms. Bautista appeared at their table with her clipboard, which everyone knew meant bad news. "Your display needs a source form signed by a parent before the office will authorize you to use images from that database," she said. "And the fair is Friday setup. I need it tomorrow."

Emile's mother worked nights. She would already be asleep by the time he got home, and she left before he woke up. A signed form was impossible, which meant no diagram, which meant going back to the sad face. He stared at his sketch, and then at his sketch again, and realized something. He did not actually need the database image. He needed the fact, and he already had the fact. The form covered the pictures, not the idea. He could draw his own door, his own keys, his own lock, all from his notebook.

That night he left his mother a note on the kitchen counter.

"Mom. I don't need the form anymore, I'm drawing everything myself. But can you look at my poster sketch on the fridge and tell me if the lock looks like a lock? I'll check before school. Love, Emile."

In the morning the sketch was still on the fridge, and next to it in her handwriting was one word: "Lockish." Underneath she had drawn a tiny arrow pointing at his door and written "add hinges, more exciting."

At setup on Friday, a kid from another class wandered past their table, chewing gum, looking indifferent to every poster in the gym. Then he stopped. "Wait," he said, pointing at the two keys Emile had cut from foil. "The brain makes its own key?"

"Acetylcholine," Emile said. "And nicotine's the fake copy that fits the same lock."

The kid leaned in and tried the foil key against the cardboard lock himself.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
story:
Avery slid her flashcards across the desk and waited for Mr. Gupta to call on someone. Around the room, her classmates in Japanese class were whispering practice sentences to each other, and the windows of room 114 rattled whenever the heater kicked on. Today's assignment was family and pets, and Avery wanted to volunteer first, because last week she had frozen when asked to count to ten and Nigel had to whisper the last three numbers to her.

"Okaasan wa yasashii desu," she said when her turn came, sitting up straight. "My mother is kind. We have a cat. Neko ga imasu." She felt pretty good about it, especially the cat part, so the silence that followed confused her. Nigel frowned at his own paper. Richard raised his hand halfway and then lowered it. Mr. Gupta just smiled and said, "Almost. Try again, and this time think about whose mother it is."

Whose mother it is? Avery stared at the word on her card. Okaasan. She had copied it from the board on Monday, when Mr. Gupta had asked Nigel about his weekend and Nigel had said something with okaasan in it. Wait, she thought. Nigel was talking about his own mother on Monday, and Mr. Gupta didn't correct him. She tested a hypothesis in her head: the same word can't be wrong for Nigel and right for me unless the rule isn't about politeness at all, but about who you're talking about. When Nigel spoke to Mr. Gupta about his mother, maybe that made her someone else's mother from the listener's point of view. Which would mean Avery needed a different word for her own.

"Is it... haha?" she asked slowly, and watched Mr. Gupta's face. He nodded once, and she said it again, louder: "Haha wa yasashii desu." Richard leaned over and whispered that he'd made the exact same mistake in his first draft, and Avery felt her ears go warm but not in a bad way. On the board, Mr. Gupta wrote the two words side by side, one for your own family and one for somebody else's, and Avery copied them with a little arrow between them so she'd remember.

After class she quizzed Nigel in the hallway. "Your little brother, mine, same rule?" she asked, and he shrugged and said probably, so they made a game of it, taking turns inventing families. Avery drew a chart in the back of her notebook, two columns, and counted her correct answers against her wrong ones until the ratio stopped mattering because the wrong ones ran out. By Friday, when Mr. Gupta asked for volunteers, her hand was up before he finished the sentence. "Haha wa yasashii desu," she said, "neko ga imasu, and Nigel-san's okaasan makes great onigiri, apparently." Nigel laughed so hard he dropped his pencil.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
story:
On her first morning at Camp Windward, Emilia learned three things: the pancake syrup was watery, the mosquitoes were generous, and every swimmer at the waterfront had to have a buddy. Amber had been assigned to her before breakfast, a girl with a sunburned nose and a whistle she'd won in a raffle, which she blew for no reason at all.

"Buddies stick together," Amber said as they walked down to the lake. "When the lifeguards blow their whistles, that's a buddy check. Every pair has to grab hands and hold them up so the staff can count everyone fast."

"Everyone? At once?" Emilia asked.

"Every single swimmer. You'll see."

The water was warm and green, and for an hour Emilia forgot to be homesick. Then she noticed something glittering in the shallows near the reeds, half sunk in the mud. It looked like a compass, or a watch, and it was definitely not hers. She waded toward it, then out of the water entirely, following the shoreline until the glittering thing turned out to be a bottle cap and the swimming area was far behind her. Somewhere a whistle blew, once, sharp. She heard it the way you hear a bird, and kept hunting for the bottle cap's imaginary owner.

The second whistle was longer. Emilia looked up and saw the lifeguards standing on the dock with clipboards, and every swimmer in the lake was holding hands with a partner, arms raised. Except for one gap in the line, one girl standing alone with her hand up and nothing to hold. Amber. Emilia's stomach seemed to dissolve on the spot. She had never seen someone look worried like that, worried in a way that was almost contagious, because now she was worried too, and she was the reason.

She ran. The gravel path had seemed short before; now it stretched like taffy. The lifeguard on the dock was already reaching for the emergency radio, and Emilia did the fastest math of her life: if she didn't get back before that call went out, boats would launch, the whole camp would be searched, and her first day would become a story told at every campfire forever.

"I'm here!" she shouted, splashing into the shallows. "I'm the missing buddy!"

Amber grabbed her hand and hauled it into the air so hard Emilia's arm nearly left its socket. The lifeguard counted the pairs, found the number matched, and lowered the radio. He did not look happy, but he did say, "Nice sprint."

Later, sitting on the dock drying off, Emilia tried to figure out her own mistake, because she wanted a criterion for first-day success she could actually meet, and "never make a mistake" was not going to be it. Maybe the rule was simpler: when you have a buddy, stay where your buddy can see you.

"So what was so important out there?" Amber asked.

"A bottle cap. I thought it was a compass."

Amber laughed so hard she had to lie back on the dock. "Tomorrow we hunt for treasure together. Deal?"

"Deal," said Emilia, and shook on it, one buddy to another.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
The line outside the arena wrapped around two whole blocks, and Jake had been in it since six in the morning. He clutched the ten dollars he had saved from mowing lawns, because the radio station had promised that the first five hundred tickets to the Silverhawks show would sell for just five dollars each. Behind him, Colt peeled off his hoodie and tied it around his waist, and Ayden shared a granola bar with a girl in front of them who had forgotten breakfast. "It's like a monsoon hit," Ayden said, watching the crowd pour in from the parking lot. "Everybody in town must be here."

"I did the math," Jake said. "The arena holds five thousand, but they're only selling five hundred of the cheap seats. After that, regular tickets are thirty-five dollars." Thirty-five was more than he had, more than he could get before Saturday. He wanted this the way you want things at twelve, completely and without excuses.

The doors opened at ten, and the line shuffled forward in short bursts. Jake watched the board above the ticket window like it was a scoreboard. Cheap seats: 412 left. Then 300. Then 178. Each time the number dropped, his stomach dropped with it. When they were still half a block from the door, the number read 61, and a boy in a Silverhawks shirt came striding out, waving his ticket like a flag. Behind him came a girl with red eyes, holding nothing. "They said there's still regular tickets," she told her mom, "but I only brought ten dollars."

That was the moment Jake understood something he couldn't see but could feel all along the sidewalk. Hundreds of people wanted the five-dollar tickets, and there were only five hundred of them, so most people in this line were going to walk away with nothing. The price was too low for how few tickets there were. "It's a shortage," Ayden said when Jake described it, because Ayden's older sister took an economics class and used words like that at dinner. "That's what they call the gap when more people want a thing than there is of the thing."

"We're not going to make it," Colt said flatly, and the board agreed: 12 left. Jake counted the people between them and the window. More than twelve. It wasn't math anymore, it was arithmetic, and arithmetic didn't care about feelings.

The girl in front of them, the one who'd forgotten breakfast, turned around. "You two want the cheap seats that bad?" She held up her phone, which showed a group chat where four friends had just bailed on her. "I'm only buying one now. You can have my spots." It wasn't charity exactly; she just didn't want to stand alone. Ayden pushed forward too, and the three of them moved up as one small knot of people.

The board said 3 when Jake reached the window. He slid his ten dollars under the glass, two tickets, one for him and one for Colt, and behind them Ayden leaned in with his crumpled five just as the number changed to 2.

"Sold out of those," the cashier said, and Ayden's face fell, but the girl who'd given up her spot was already turning around. "Hey," she said, "my friends aren't coming. Want to participate in being my ticket buddy? You pay for the popcorn."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Arthur stood on the porch of Mathis's house holding a box of oranges, and he could not figure out one thing: why was there a row of shoes sitting by the front door? Sneakers, sandals, little canvas shoes, all lined up neatly on a raised ledge, pointing outward. Behind him, his phone buzzed. It was a message from Blakely: "Party starts at 3 SHARP. Mathis's grandma flew in last night and she's making dinner. Do NOT be late, she counts late people. Also did you bring a gift? His family does gifts."

Arthur typed back fast. "Yes oranges. Why does it matter?" Blakely answered with a single line: "Just knock and copy what I do when you get here. 3 sharp." It was 2:54. He had six minutes, and he still did not understand the shoes.

He knocked. Mathis's mother opened the door, smiled, and looked down at Arthur's sneakers, then at the empty spot on the ledge. Arthur remembered his social studies teacher once saying you could quantify a custom by counting how many people followed it, and here the count was perfect: every single shoe in that row was off a foot. No exceptions. He tested his idea right there on the mat. He crouched, unlaced his sneakers, and set them beside a pair of small blue slippers that seemed to be waiting for him, toes pointing out like all the others.

"You figured out the genkan," Mathis said from the hallway, grinning. "That's what we call the entrance where shoes come off. Most people just stand there looking confused." He held out his hand, and Arthur remembered the other thing Blakely had warned him about, so he offered the oranges with both hands instead of one. Mathis's mother received them the same way, with both hands and a small bow, and Arthur copied the bow, probably too deep, because Mathis laughed.

At dinner, Arthur watched before he moved. Mathis's grandmother lifted her bowl of rice, so Arthur lifted his. Nobody stuck chopsticks upright into the rice, so Arthur laid his across the little rest when he paused, which Blakely, arriving breathless at 3:02, did not do. Blakely reached across the table for the soy sauce, and Arthur slid it toward him quietly before the grandmother's frown could finish forming.

"Nice save," Blakely whispered.

After the cake, Mathis's grandmother said something to Mathis, who translated with pink ears. "She says you eat like you've been here before. And she wants to know if you'll come back next Saturday." Arthur looked down at the blue slippers on his feet, then at the row of shoes waiting by the door.

"Tell her yes," Arthur said. "I'll wear the easy sneakers."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
Julia had been looking forward to this all week: her first real babysitting job, at Ms. Thompson's house, with two-year-old Benjy. She had even made a schedule, which felt very professional. Everything went beautifully until Benjy decided to mash his spaghetti into his hair, his ears, and somehow one eyebrow, and Julia announced, with great pride, "Bath time."

She ran the water and tested it with her elbow, exactly the way her mom had shown her. She set out the towel. She had just lowered Benjy into the shallow tub, where he sat happily patting the water like a drum, when the phone in the hallway rang and rang and would not stop. Julia remembered something her mom had said once, something so fundamental that Julia had thought it was strange at the time: a young child can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out, so a child should never be left alone in or near a bath. Julia had pictured drowning as loud and splashy. Her mom had said no, it could be silent, and that was exactly why you never, ever stepped away, not even for a phone.

"Okay, buddy," Julia said. She scooped Benjy out of the tub, wrapped him in the big towel like a burrito, and carried the whole soggy burrito down the hallway with her, dripping all over the rug. Benjy thought this was hilarious. "Bah," he said, pointing at the phone.

It was Ms. Thompson. "Julia! I tried the house phone because my mobile network keeps dropping calls tonight. Is everything all right? I heard the water running." Julia explained, in one breathless sentence, about the spaghetti and the bath and the ringing. She did not mention the burrito. "I brought him with me," she added, and Ms. Thompson paused, then said, "Good girl. I'll be home in ten minutes. Don't put him back in the water unless you're staying right beside him."

The twist came at the door. Ms. Thompson walked in holding a small camera, a doorbell one, and said, "I could see the hallway on my phone. The whole phone call, the whole burrito." She grinned. "Do you know how many sitters leave the kid in the tub? My sister's a swim teacher, and she says it's her mission to teach this stuff, like planting seeds and waiting for them to germinate. You already had the seed."

Julia stood taller, towel-warmed toddler on her hip, spaghetti still lodged in one eyebrow. "So," she said, "same time next Friday?"

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
story:
Jaxson sat on the low wall by the basketball courts with his right arm propped on his knee, the cast running from his palm to below his elbow. He had gotten it eleven days ago at the skate park, when the board shot out from under him on the ramp and he threw his hand out to catch himself. The doctor in the emergency room had looked at the X-ray on the light board and said, "Broken radius, right near the wrist." His whole wrist had been sore and swollen before that, so puffy he couldn't move his thumb.

At lunch, Karina dropped onto the wall beside him and peeled a sunflower seed with her teeth, spitting the hull into the dirt. "My brother did the exact same thing last year," she said. "Fell off his bike, caught himself with his hand, broke the radius near his wrist."

"Same bone?" Jaxson asked.

"Same spot. The doctor told him it's the most common fracture in kids. They see it all the time."

Jaxson started a list on his phone with his left thumb: himself, Karina's brother. At recess, Ibrahim came over from the soccer game to sign the cast, and Jaxson asked him if he'd ever broken anything. "Wrist," Ibrahim said. "Skiing. I stuck my arm out when I fell." Jaxson added him. By the end of the day the list had three more names, and every single one was a radius near the wrist, from a fall onto an outstretched hand. He sat with that fact for a while, turning it over. It couldn't be a coincidence five times in a row. Something invisible connected all of them.

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before the cast came off. "Karina," he said when she found him after last period, "everybody on my list did the same thing when they fell. They put a hand out."

"So?"

"So the bone doesn't break from the fall itself. It breaks from the catching." He stood up. "Watch. I'm going to teach the little kids at the playground how to fall."

There was a climbing structure shaped like a ship, and the first graders went down its slide too fast and tumbled off the end. Jaxson stood where they landed and demonstrated with his good arm: bend your knees, tuck your chin, land on your side and forearm, never a straight arm. The kids thought falling practice was a game. One boy named Dylan did it seven times in a row on purpose, laughing so hard the laughter turned contagious and soon half the playground was throwing themselves onto the wood chips in tidy rolls.

A week later Ms. Sutherland stopped Jaxson in the hallway. "Odd thing," she said. "Two winters running I've sent someone to the office with a broken wrist off that slide. Nothing this week, not even a scraped palm."

Jaxson nodded and kept walking, left hand pressed over his cast pocket, where the list now had a second column of tally marks under the words DID NOT STICK HAND OUT. Through the window he could see the wood chips glitter where the sun refracted off a piece of bottle glass, and Dylan, mid-roll, coming down the side of the slide.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Painting wet-on-wet, putting paint onto paper that is still wet, makes the colour spread with soft, blurry edges instead of crisp ones.
story:
Mathis taped a sheet of heavy paper to the kitchen table and set out two jars of water, one for rinsing and one that he tried to keep clean. His assignment from Mr. Farah was a portrait in watercolour, built in layers from the lightest wash to the darkest, and it was due on Friday. So far he had a pale oval for a face and not much else.

Violet came over after school with her own brushes rolled in a dish towel. She was painting her grandmother, and she had already ruined two sheets. "The face is fine," she said, flattening her paper beside his. "It's the background that's wrong. I wanted it soft, like a haze of leaves behind her. Instead I got sharp stripes."

Mathis leaned over to look. Her strokes had dried with hard edges, each one outlined where the pigment had settled. His own background, painted in a hurry, had gone the opposite way, blooming into soft clouds that drifted up over the edge of his face oval. He frowned at it, then at hers, then at the paper itself, as if the answer were hidden somewhere between the fibres.

"Wait," he said. "I painted mine right after I wet the whole sheet. You painted yours on dry paper, didn't you?" Violet nodded. He dampened a scrap with clean water, touched one brushstroke of green onto the wet part and one onto the dry part, and set the scrap flat where they could both watch. On the wet half, the colour crept outward, its edges going soft and blurry like breath on a window. On the dry half, the stroke stayed crisp. "It's called wet-on-wet," Mathis said. "Painting onto paper that's still wet makes the colour spread."

Violet grabbed a fresh sheet and a wide brush. She wet the whole background around where her grandmother's head would go, then dropped in greens and a little yellow, and the colours melted into each other into something lush, like a garden seen through summer heat. "That's it," she breathed. "That's exactly what I wanted." She decided she would incorporate the trick into all her future backgrounds, and she said she might even sell small portraits at the winter craft fair, though Mathis pointed out that one sale of eight dollars was not exactly revenue.

He went back to his own portrait with the scrap test still drying beside him. Now he understood why his first attempt had gone cloudy, and he worked the other way around: he let the face dry completely, then built the shadows on the nose and under the jaw in small, controlled layers, each one darker than the last. The nose finally looked like a nose.

By the time his mother called them for sandwiches, Violet's grandmother sat in her green haze, and Mathis had a real face with dark hair laid in over the last pale layer. He pulled the tape from the edges of his sheet and held the portrait up to the window light. "Look at that," he said. "Mr. Farah is going to think I paid someone."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Places, people and routines linked with nicotine use, such as a certain time of day, can become cues that trigger cravings on their own.
story:
Samuel stood at the whiteboard with his marker hovering, because the diagram still had a hole in it. On Friday, Mr. Saleh had asked each group to teach the class one thing about how nicotine changes the brain, and Samuel had volunteered to explain the reward pathway, the part where nicotine tricks the brain into repeating something that is not actually rewarding. He had drawn it meticulously, every arrow in place, but his notes only went as far as "then cravings happen." He could not say why cravings showed up long after the nicotine was gone. Cristiano and Matteo were counting on him, and he had nothing.

At lunch, Cristiano slid his tray next to Samuel's. "Maybe cravings just hibernate," he said, "like a bear, and wake up when they feel like it." Samuel shook his head. His grandfather had quit smoking years before Samuel was even born, and last weekend Samuel had noticed something strange. Every morning, Grandpa drank his coffee standing at the kitchen window, and every morning, for just a second, his hand drifted toward his shirt pocket, the pocket where the cigarettes used to live. Then he would catch himself and wrap both hands around the mug. Samuel had said nothing, but the gesture had stuck in his mind like a splinter.

He tested it that evening with a question. "Grandpa, what would happen if I made your coffee somewhere else, like in the living room?" His grandfather looked at him for a long moment. "Funny you ask," he said. "Your grandmother made it on the porch last spring, and I didn't think about cigarettes once. Same coffee, same morning." Samuel felt the hole in his diagram closing. It was not the coffee. It was the place, the routine, the time of day. Those things had hitched themselves to the old habit, and now they could pull the craving out all by themselves, even after years with no nicotine at all.

On presentation day, Mr. Saleh leaned against his desk and watched. Samuel drew the pathway, then drew a clock, a window, a mug beside it. "Places, people, and routines linked with nicotine use," he said, "like a certain time of day, can become cues that trigger cravings on their own." He told them about the pocket, the window, the porch. Matteo raised his hand. "So the brain is like a consumer that got tricked once, and keeps paying?" Samuel grinned. "Basically."

After class, Mr. Saleh caught Samuel at the door. "Where did the pocket part come from?" he asked. Samuel told him about his grandfather, and how for a moment this morning, in the car outside school, Samuel had reached for a water bottle that was not there and realized he always grabbed one at that same corner. "It works for everything," Samuel said. "Good habits too." Mr. Saleh laughed and held the door open. "Careful, or you'll be standing at the whiteboard every morning for the rest of your life."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Average speed equals distance travelled divided by the time taken.
story:
The problem started because Reuben's marble, an obstinate hunk of green glass he called The Tank, kept losing to Kaylee's silver one on the plywood ramp, and Reuben insisted it was only because the ramp was crooked. Declan didn't care whose marble won. He cared that by Monday he had to hand Mr. Torres a graph, a real one with axes and points, and he had promised it would show something measured, not guessed.

"Then let's settle it," Kaylee said, unrolling a tape measure across the grass. "We time them over the same distance and figure out who's really faster."

They dragged the ramp to the top of the picnic table so the marbles would roll a long way across the lawn. Reuben wanted to race first and think later, but Declan laid a ruler across the grass like a finish line and said no, they needed numbers first. Kaylee held her phone stopwatch. Reuben crouched like a sprinter at the start, which was ridiculous, and released The Tank.

"Four metres," Declan called, checking the tape, "in two and a half seconds." He wrote it in his notebook. "So that's four divided by two and a half." He worked it out. "One point six. Metres every second."

"Metres per second," Kaylee said. "That's the average speed. Distance travelled divided by the time taken." She said it like she was reading it off a cereal box, casual, but Declan grabbed the pencil and wrote the words down before she could change her mind about sharing them.

They ran each marble five times. The silver one crossed four metres in two seconds flat, which made it two metres per second every single run. The Tank wobbled between one point four and one point seven. "It's not the ramp," Declan said, turning the notebook so Reuben could see the columns. "Your marble is just slower on average."

Reuben picked up The Tank and glared at it. "He needs nurturing," he announced. "Polish. Motivation." Kaylee snorted so hard she had to sit down in the grass.

Declan drew the graph anyway. He put time along the bottom and distance up the side, then plotted each run of the silver marble, and the dots climbed in a straight line. The Tank's dots sagged below it like a tired staircase. He drew two smooth lines through them and labelled each one. It was the first homework he'd ever been excited to hand in, and he knew this because he had asked his mom to drive him to school early, which she'd called a privilege and he'd called not wanting to wait.

Monday morning, Mr. Torres held the graph up to the window light. "Whose line is this bottom one?"

"The Tank's," Declan said. "He's being nurtured."

Behind him, Reuben raised his hand and said, "I demand a rematch at eight metres."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can also show up in behaviour, such as snapping at friends, having trouble concentrating or losing interest in hobbies, and noticing these signs is the first step to managing it.
story:
Piper stood in aisle three of Mr. Iyer's pharmacy, holding two boxes of sleep tea and reading the back of each one like it was a test question. "Chamomile," she muttered. "Also chamomile. Why do you even exist, second box?"

"You are talking to the tea," said Andy, who had followed her in after school.

"I'm performing quality control." She put the second box back with unnecessary force, and a whole row of cough drops rattled. Then she heard herself and winced. She'd snapped at Andy three times since Friday, once because he'd asked what time it was. Who snapped at somebody for asking the time?

Mr. Iyer came around the counter, keys jingling. "Piper, your mother called. She wants you to pick up the refill for your grandmother, and also, what did poor Andy do?"

"Nothing," Piper said. "That's the weird part." She handed over the prescription slip and, while he fetched it, stared at the shelf. Last week she'd quit the piano piece she'd been excited about for a month, told her teacher it was boring. She'd also read the same social studies paragraph four times and still couldn't have said what it said. She'd been revising for the piano exam, too, and sleeping about four hours a night. Hmm, she thought. Snapping at friends, couldn't concentrate, quit the thing she loved. Was there a pattern hiding underneath all that, one invisible cause behind three different problems?

In October she'd watched her cousin Timothy do exactly the same thing at their grandmother's house. He'd yelled at the dog for existing, then at her for passing the rice, and finally slumped at the table and said, "I've been stressed about hockey tryouts all week. I didn't even notice until I just snapped at everybody for no reason." Even the dog had looked skeptical.

"Mr. Iyer," she said slowly, "if someone couldn't concentrate, and got bored of stuff they usually love, and yelled at people over nothing, would you say maybe those are signs of stress showing up in how you act?"

He set the refill bag on the counter. "I would say noticing the signs is the first step to managing them. And I would say the chamomile is on your mother's list, and the tea won't work if you fall asleep at three in the morning anyway."

"Timothy said to breathe like a box," Andy offered. "In four, hold, out four. He does it before face-offs. He looks like a confused blowfish, but he says it works."

"That's because he is a confused blowfish," Piper said, but she tried it right there, in four, hold, out four, next to the cough drops. Her shoulders came down an inch, like they'd been waiting for permission. She picked up the tea, the refill, and a notebook so she could actually plan her sleep like a normal human instead of a raccoon.

At the door she paused. "Andy, sorry about the time thing on Friday."

"It's fine. You want to come Saturday? Grandma's making her authentic dal, the real heritage recipe with the scary chilies."

"Only if Timothy breathes like a blowfish first."

"Deal," said Andy, and pushed the door open into the cold.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Repeating a measurement several times and taking the average gives a more reliable result than a single try.
story:
Claire had taped a ruler to the hallway floor, angled a clipboard against the wall, and was on her knees trying to hold a marble still on a ramp made of a cereal box. The plan was simple: roll the ball, time it, divide distance by time, and draw a distance-time graph. Ms. Pérez had promised that whoever produced the cleanest graph would get the front table at the science fair, and Claire intended to thwart Paige's plan to win it with a volcano.

"It's a stopwatch, not a laser," Paige said from the stairs, where she had come to watch and, Claire suspected, to spy. "You don't have to aim it."

"Very funny. Say go."

The marble rolled thirty centimetres in one point two seconds. Then again in one point one. Then again in one point one. Claire wrote the numbers in her most assertive handwriting, the kind that said this data is final.

On the fourth try, the reading said four point nine seconds. Claire stared at it. The marble could not have rolled thirty centimetres in five seconds unless it had stopped to think. She checked the floor. She checked the stopwatch. The cat was asleep on the stairs, so it wasn't the cat.

"That one's wrong," Paige said. "Throw it out."

"You can't just throw out data you don't like. That's like deleting the ugly part of your face in a photo." Claire reread her notes and found the problem. On the fourth try she had been mid-sneeze when she hit the button. The timer had started late and the marble had finished its whole journey before she stopped it. One bad try, one wild number.

She rolled the marble nine more times, recording each one, and added up the whole column. Then she divided. The average came out to one point one two seconds, almost exactly what the good readings had said all along. The single sneeze number, sitting in a sea of repeats, had barely moved it. She wrote "average of 12 trials" on the graph and started plotting points, and the line came out so straight it looked drawn with a ruler, which, in a way, it had been.

At the fair, Ms. Pérez paused at Claire's table and frowned at one card in particular. "Trial four. Nearly five seconds?"

"Sneeze," Claire said.

Ms. Pérez looked at the averaging note, then at the straight line, and made a small mark on her clipboard. Paige, at the volcano table next door, leaned over. "My eruption starts in two minutes. Want to time it?"

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
The moving truck left tracks in the mud outside 14 Kettle Street, and Zack stood on the porch watching it go. His mom had said the neighbors would come by, but by dinner nobody had, and by the next morning the only person he'd met was Mr. Njoroge, who lived two doors down and had waved once while filling his bird feeder. Zack wanted one friend before school started on Monday. That gave him four days.

He tried the obvious move first. He walked the whole street, all the way to the dead end where a translucent plastic tarp flapped over somebody's half-built shed, and rang three doorbells. A parent answered each one and said their kid was out. Zack noticed something on the way back. There were two kids about his age on the street, from what he'd seen: a boy skateboarding in the driveway of number 9, and a girl watering plants at number 21. He lived at 14. Number 9 was five houses away. Number 21 was seven. Neither one had come near him.

Then he remembered something his older cousin had told him last summer, back when the cousin was home from college. "There was this study in 1950," she had said, munching chips on the porch steps. "A student housing complex at MIT. Leon Festinger and some colleagues. They found the residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them." Zack had shrugged at the time. Now he stood in his driveway and thought about it. It wasn't about who was nicest or who had the best skateboard. It was about distance. If he wanted a friend fast, he had to shrink the distance, and the closest kid to him wasn't on this street at all. It was whoever lived in the blue house directly behind his fence.

The back gate hinge squeaked when he pushed through it into the alley. A boy was out there re-taping a hockey stick, wind drafting through the alley and lifting the tape from his hand. "You live in the blue house?" Zack asked. The boy looked up. "Yousuf. You just moved in. I heard your dog." They ended up shooting a tennis ball against the garage door for an hour, and Yousuf said his friend Noemi from number 21 was coming over Saturday, and that Zack should come too, because her mom made the best samosas on the street.

Saturday afternoon Zack climbed the fence again, because by then it was the fastest route and it felt like the right one. Yousuf was already in the alley with Noemi, who held a plate wrapped in foil. "You took the back way," she said. "Smart. Everyone on this street does, eventually."

"Tape's coming off your stick again," Zack said, and tossed him the roll.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Piper balanced the bowl on the counter of Gran's cramped kitchen, the one that smelled like cinnamon and old newspapers. Gran was resting her bad hip in the armchair, so tonight's bread was Piper's job, and she intended to make it perfect. Tobin had come along, mostly for the promise of warm crust with butter, and he sat on the stool by the window fanning himself with a dish towel.

"You know what would be radical?" Tobin said. "Swirling honey into the top before it bakes. Like a spiral."

"First it has to rise," Piper said. "That's the part I keep thinking about." She had read the recipe twice on the bus, and one line had stuck with her: yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles. That was why you kneaded it, to build the web that held the bubbles in. She liked knowing that the puffy loaf was really thousands of tiny pockets of gas, made by something alive eating sugar.

She stirred the yeast into water from the kettle, added flour, and set the bowl near the warm stove to rise. Then she and Tobin played cards at the table, and Gran called out advice from her chair about which tricks Tobin was falling for. He lost three hands in a row and demanded a treaty: no more whispering between the two of them, since Gran's coaching clearly counted as cheating.

An hour later, Piper peeked under the towel and her stomach dropped. The dough sat flat and dense, exactly the size she had left it. She pressed one finger into the top and the dent stayed, like poking clay.

"It's dead," she said. "Something killed it."

Tobin leaned over the bowl and sniffed. "Smells like nothing. Like wet flour."

Piper stood still, running through the steps. She had used the flour, the salt, the spoonful of sugar the recipe called for. Then she touched the side of the kettle, still faintly warm, and her mind jumped backward. She had poured water straight from the kettle because she was in a hurry. Hot water. She thought about the yeast as something alive, something eating and breathing, and realized she might have boiled it before it ever got to eat anything. She had no way to see inside those tiny specks, but she could test the idea.

She filled a glass with cool water, added a splash from the kettle, and tested it against her wrist the way Gran tested milk for babies. Warm but not stinging. She mixed fresh yeast with a pinch of sugar and set the glass beside the bowl. "If it's the water," she said, "this should foam up." Ten minutes later a tan froth had crept over the top of the glass, and Tobin poked her arm. "Look, it's alive. That's the gas, right? From eating the sugar?"

"That's the gas," Piper said, already measuring flour again. She had to prioritize the new batch over the card game now, because Gran needed bread for supper and the oven had to be hot by five. Tobin abandoned the cards without being asked and greased the pan while she kneaded, folding and pressing until her arms ached and the dough felt smooth as an earlobe.

The second bowl rose like a slow tide, swelling over its rim while the kitchen filled with a bready, yeasty smell. Gran limped in just as Piper slashed the top and slid it into the oven. "The first dough didn't rise at all," Piper told her. "I killed the yeast with water straight from the kettle. It was too hot for them."

Gran chuckled and squeezed her shoulder. "My mother did the same thing her first winter married. Whole village teased her for a year." Tobin drizzled the honey into a spiral, careful and slow, and when the loaf came out craggy and golden, he cut the first slice while it was still steaming and carried it to Gran's chair. Piper took the heel, the best part, and pressed it flat under the butter knife.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Jaxon set the guitar on his lap for the third time that afternoon and pressed his left fingertips against the strings. They flared hot, the way they had every day since Monday, and he put the instrument down again. "I'm done," he told Anaeve, who was tuning her flute one chair over in the band room. "A week of this and my fingers feel like I slammed them in a door."

"You can't quit," Anaeve said. "Mr. Hoffmann already put you in the program for the concert Friday. He did a whole census of who plays what, and you're the only guitar."

Lindsey looked up from her trumpet. "My brother plays guitar. He says his fingers used to hurt too, and then they just stopped. He called it getting calluses."

Jaxon frowned at his fingertips. They didn't look different from anyone else's. He tried to think of another explanation, something hidden. Maybe the strings were defective. Maybe his hands were shaped wrong. But Lindsey's brother played the same kind of guitar and didn't hurt anymore, so the strings were probably fine, and hands didn't come in a special guitar shape. The difference had to be time. His fingers hurt now, in the present, but something invisible might be building underneath.

"Okay," he said slowly. "A test. If I practice a little every single day until Friday, maybe something changes. If nothing changes, I quit after the concert."

"Modified experiment," Lindsey said, pointing her trumpet at him. "I'll take notes."

Mr. Hoffmann poked his head in from the hallway. "Rehearsal at lunch tomorrow, everyone. And Jaxon, that chord progression needs to be smooth by Friday, not a series of accidents."

The next two days were rough. Jaxon practiced during lunch, then again at home until his mom asked if he was secretly nocturnal, playing in the dark after bedtime. Each session stung at first, then settled into a dull ache he could ignore. By Thursday afternoon, he noticed something odd. The strings felt sharp under his fingers when he started, but by the middle of a song, he stopped thinking about them at all.

On Friday morning, before the concert, Lindsey grabbed his hand and turned it over, inspecting his fingertips like a detective. "There. Feel that? The skin's tougher there now."

Jaxon ran his thumb across the ridges. The sore spots had hardened, and pressing the strings barely registered anymore. "So it was real," he said. "It just took days to show up."

"Regretting your quitting speech?" Anaeve asked.

"Maybe," Jaxon said. "Ask me after the concert."

When his turn came, he played the progression clean, every chord landing where it should, and afterward he sat in the chair still holding the guitar, pressing one string slowly with his thumb, then doing it again.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.
story:
Vincent carried the cardboard carrier out of the Sunnyside Animal Shelter with both hands, the way Ms. Kim had shown him, because inside it a brown guinea pig named Biscuit was riding home to his apartment for the very first time. Amine walked beside him, jingling the volunteer badge in his pocket; he had logged ten Saturdays at the shelter to earn that badge, and he wanted to log ten more. "You got the good one," Amine said, peering through the air holes. "Biscuit is the friendliest of the whole small-animal room. Some of them are totally indifferent to people, but not him."

For the first two days everything went fine. Biscuit ate lettuce from Vincent's palm and popcorned around the cage, hopping in little jumps. Then, on the third night, Vincent heard a sound like a tiny metal saw. Ting, ting, ting. He crept to the cage and watched Biscuit grab the bars with his teeth and pull. Ting. Vincent lay awake listening, and by morning he had a theory: Biscuit could not be hungry, because the food bowl was still half full, and he could not be lonely, because he did the gnawing even while Vincent sat right there. Something else had to be behind it.

At school, Vincent found Amine at lunch and slid his tray down next to him. "Biscuit chews the bars all night. He's not hungry and he's not scared. What else makes an animal chew?" Amine turned his milk carton around in his hands, thinking. "You know who would know? Ms. Kim. Come Saturday, I'm volunteering anyway. I could use another pair of hands, too, the dog kennels take forever to dismantle when we deep-clean them."

Saturday morning, Ms. Kim was restacking hay in the small-animal room when they found her. Vincent described the bar chewing, the full food bowl, the midnight noise. Ms. Kim nodded and pointed at the row of hutches, each one holding a chew block, a willow stick, or a piece of untreated wood. "Their front teeth never stop growing," she said. "They need things to chew on to wear them down." Vincent felt the insight land like a puzzle piece snapping into place. The shelter animals all had wood to gnaw, and none of them touched their bars. Biscuit had nothing in his cage but food, hay, and a little plastic house.

That afternoon, Vincent's dad drove them to the pet store, where Amine helped him pick out applewood sticks and a plain wooden tunnel. When they got home, Vincent arranged the sticks in a corner and set Biscuit inside the tunnel. Biscuit's nose twitched once, twice. Then he gripped an applewood stick in his front teeth and began to chew, a soft wooden crunch instead of the tinny ting of bars. Amine grinned and pulled out his phone to log his eleventh Saturday. "Eleven," he said, snapping a picture of Biscuit happily gnawing away. "Nine to go."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Penelope sat on the cold metal bleachers with her notebook open on her knees, because the junior varsity game before hers was still going and she had a problem to solve. Two of her cousins had sent her links that morning. One said her team's free throw shooting had gone up 10 points since last season. The other said it had gone up 25 percent. Both stories had a photo of the same gym, the same buzzer, even the same watermark. Ten and twenty-five. Somebody had to be wrong, and Penelope suspected it was both of them.

"Stop doing math at a basketball game," said Kesler, dropping onto the bench beside her with a bag of popcorn.

"I'm not doing math. I'm doing detective work."

James leaned over from her other side, popcorn breath and all. "My dad read that first one out loud at breakfast. He said ten. Then he read the other one and said twenty-five, and then he made this face like the news was lying to him on purpose."

The scoreboard rattled through a time-out. Down on the court, the junior varsity guard missed her fourth free throw of the quarter, and the gym exhaled all at once, a long sad whoosh of two hundred people. Penelope wrote 40 at the top of her page. Last season, according to the stats her mom had printed from the league site, the team had made about 40 percent of its free throws. This season the sheet said 50 percent. She wrote that too, and then drew a line between them.

"So wait," she said slowly, tapping the pen. "It went from forty to fifty. That's ten more. Out of a hundred, that's ten percentage points, so the first story is right." Kesler opened his mouth and she held up a finger. "But. Fifty is twenty-five more than forty, because a quarter of forty is ten. So it also went up by twenty-five percent, and the second story is right too."

"Both of them?" James said. "They can't both be right. They sound like different amounts."

"They're the same amount wearing different coats." She underlined 40 and 50 twice. "Ten points, twenty-five percent, same change."

Mr. Farah came up the bleachers two steps at a time, whistle around his neck, clipboard under his arm. He had coached at this school long enough to have opinions about everything, including the heating, the landlord who controlled the heating, and the reporter from the community paper who, he said, treated the team's press box like fertile ground for whatever number sounded most dramatic that week.

"Coach," Penelope called down. "The paper said we went up ten. The other paper said twenty-five. Which one's the lie?"

Mr. Farah squinted at her notebook, then at the court, then back at the notebook. "Neither. Going from forty percent to fifty percent is ten percentage points and twenty-five percent at the same time. Reporters just pick whichever sounds bigger." He tapped the clipboard. "Now stop interviewing me and get your ankles taped. You're starting."

The buzzer went off. Kesler stole the last of the popcorn. Penelope shoved the notebook into her bag, where the page would wrinkle into something she could photograph later and send to both cousins at once.

"Same amount, different coats," she muttered, lacing up.

"Louder," said James.

"Nothing," she said, and ran down onto the court.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant, in his 1958 book 'The Uses of Argument'.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like burnt toast and coffee, which meant he had been up since five arguing with the toaster again. Abigail spread her debate notes across the table, right over his crossword.

"I keep losing," she said. "Ms. Rosen says my case falls apart the second anyone pushes back."

Grandpa peered at her notes over his glasses. "So build one that doesn't. What are you arguing?"

"That our town should conserve more water, even in rainy years."

"Fine. Claim. Evidence. Go."

"That's what I have." She slid the page toward him. "Claim, two pieces of evidence, done."

He read it, then slid it back. "Here's your problem. You say the reservoirs drop every August, and you say we should conserve water. But you never connect them. Why does the first fact prove the second one?"

Abigail stared at the paper. He was right. She had two things sitting side by side like strangers on a bus.

She remembered the tournament in March, standing in a hallway afterward while Linda searched her own bag for gum. A boy from another school had wandered over, still holding his flow pad, and asked why everyone kept saying "warrant" like it was obvious. "Where does the word even come from?" Linda had shrugged, but the boy knew. "The British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described his model of argument, including claim, data and warrant, in his 1958 book 'The Uses of Argument,'" he said, and then, because Linda kept digging through her bag, he added, "Basically a warrant is the bridge between your data and your claim." Abigail had written it on her hand in pen, then sweated it off by round three.

Now, at the kitchen table, she got it. "The warrant is the hidden part," she said slowly. "It's the rule underneath. Like, reservoirs drop in August because summer heat dries them out, and a town that drains its reservoirs has no backup. If there's a drought, or if refugees settle here and the population jumps, we'd need that water."

"Refugees?" Grandpa raised an eyebrow. "Sneaking that in for the sympathy vote?"

"It's evidence, not a tearjerker. The city council report says population could grow." She grabbed a fresh index card and wrote, Warrant: dropping reservoirs plus growing demand equals future shortage. She underlined it twice. "And in cross-examination, nobody can knock down the bridge if I actually build it."

Grandpa smiled and turned back to his crossword. "Seven letters, ominous, starts with S."

"Sinister," Abigail said without looking up. She was already rewriting her second point, this time with all three pieces stacked together, when the toaster popped again and set off the smoke alarm. Grandpa waved a dish towel at it like he was surrendering.

"You know," Abigail said, shouting over the beeping, "your toaster has a warrant too. It's called a repair manual."

"Mine's called a hammer," said Grandpa.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, verbs used with thou usually end in -est, so "thou knowest" means "you know".
story:
Nathaniel slid the battered copy of Romeo and Juliet across the library table and dropped into the chair beside Paige, who was already reading the same scene with her eyebrows knotted together. Ms. Fortin's assignment was due Friday: pick a scene, paraphrase every speech into modern English, and perform it with a partner. The librarian had set them up at the corner table by the window, where the afternoon light fell across the pages.

"I can't do this," Paige said. "What does this even say? 'Thou knowest my father's will hath stopped me.'" She jabbed a finger at the line. "It's like a different language."

Nathaniel squinted at it. He knew the words individually, or most of them, but strung together they turned into fog. He read the speech again, slower this time, and something snagged his attention. Knowest. Dost. Art. Wilt. Everywhere Romeo said thou, the verb grew a strange tail.

"Wait," he said, and pulled a pencil from his backpack. "Look. Thou knowest. Thou dost. Thou art." He wrote the three phrases in the margin. "It's always like that. Thou plus a word ending in e-s-t." He tested it against the next line, then the one after, like checking a combination lock. "So thou art means you are. Thou knowest means you know. It works every single time."

Paige leaned over his shoulder. "So when Juliet says 'thou wilt'," she said slowly, "that's just you will?"

"That's it." Nathaniel grinned and flipped the page. "Ms. Fortin said the paraphrase has to sound like us, like something we'd actually say. So Romeo isn't saying fancy stuff, he's just saying you a lot."

They worked through the scene line by line, and Paige read each modern version out loud to test it against her ear. When a paraphrase sounded stiff, she rewrote it right there on the scrap paper the librarian brought them, along with two juice boxes she said someone had left behind in the break room, though she set them down with a small smile. A boy at the next table kept glancing over, and finally Nathaniel waved him closer. "You stuck on the same thing? Watch this. Thou plus e-s-t. It's the whole trick."

The boy, a small kid clutching a copy of A Midsummer Night's Dream, copied the rule onto his hand in purple pen. By the time the lights blinked for closing, Nathaniel and Paige had a full script of modern dialogue, divided fairly since neither of them wanted to delegate the good lines to the other. Paige read the last speech aloud, quiet and steady, and Nathaniel nodded.

"That," he said, "is a significant improvement over yesterday."

"Yesterday we had nothing," Paige said, and laughed, gathering the pages. "Tomorrow we practice in the gym."

"Deal," Nathaniel said, and slid the book back onto the returns cart himself.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The protagonist is a story's main character, and the antagonist is the character or force working against them; their conflict drives the plot toward the climax.
story:
Emmett stared at his notebook, where his story had stopped at four lines. The writing club met in the school library every Thursday, and today Ms. Nkosi had given them forty minutes to draft a short scene with dialogue and a climax. His dialogue looked wrong. He had written, "'Get out of the snow,' she said." Then he'd tried it without the comma and it looked wrong too, so he'd coordinated his two attempts by copying Amelya's opening from across the table, one comma and one period at a time.

"Are you borrowing my punctuation?" Amelya asked.

"Coordinating," Emmett said. "There's a difference."

Colten leaned over. "Your climax is a guy standing in a driveway. That's not a climax, that's waiting for a bus."

"My climax is coming," Emmett said. "My protagonist just has to get to it." He knew that word, at least. The protagonist was the main character, his kid stuck outside in a blizzard. The problem was that nothing was stopping him. He walked through the snow. He arrived. Even Emmett could tell it was boring, and he had written it.

Amelya read it anyway, all eleven lines. "Who's working against him?"

"Nobody yet. I was going to add a grumpy neighbor."

"Don't add the neighbor," Colten said, which started a small controversy at their table about whether grumpy neighbors were allowed in fiction at all. Emmett ignored them. He looked at his story again. His kid couldn't see the road. The wind had pushed him off it twice. The snow kept filling in his footprints like it wanted to erase him.

He sat up. The storm. The storm was the one working against the protagonist the whole time. He hadn't needed a villain at all.

He flipped the page and wrote fast. "'Which way is the house?' he shouted, but the wind took the words sideways." The kid's brother was obstinate about waiting inside, so the kid had to find the door himself, and the snow got deeper with every step. At the top of the last paragraph, the kid's mittened hand hit the porch railing. Emmett underlined it twice. That was the moment everything turned, the peak of the whole thing, and he'd finally reached it.

"What's it called?" Amelya asked.

"'The Antagonist Is Weather,'" Emmett said, and handed it to Ms. Nkosi before he could change his mind.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
Luke refreshed the page for the fourth time and watched his sneaker listing sit there like a stone. Forty-two views, zero offers. He had typed the price himself, sixty dollars, because a video he'd watched said the same pair once sold for that much. His bike's bent front wheel waited in the garage, and the repair shop wanted fifty-five.

"You put sixty on those?" Sonny leaned over his shoulder at the lunch table. "Nobody's even bidding. There's like eight other pairs on there right now."

"Mine are cleaner," Luke said, though he hadn't actually checked the other listings. That night he did. Eight pairs, most listed between thirty and forty dollars, and two of them looked just as clean as his. He lowered his price to fifty and went to his English homework, copying a poem for class and counting each stanza as he went. Three stanzas, then bed.

In the morning he had one offer, for thirty-eight dollars. He closed it without answering and walked to school in a mood he tried to shake off. In science, Ms. Reddy had them testing unknown liquids, drip by drip, and he found himself thinking about his listing the same way. Something invisible was pushing the price around, and he wanted to see it clearly instead of guessing.

At lunch he laid it out for Sonny and Phillip. "There's a bunch of pairs for sale and only a few people buying. So the price has to drop until the buyers match up with the sellers. If it goes too low, everything sells out in an hour. Too high, and stuff just sits there."

Phillip nodded slowly. "My cousin calls that the equilibrium price. Market-clearing, he says, because the market gets cleared out, everything sells."

The words fit what Luke had watched happen, so he took them as a hypothesis to test. He set his price at forty-two, just above the cheapest listings but below most of them, and told himself he would leave it alone for two full days. On the first day he got three offers. One was for thirty, which he declined, and two were at forty-two. He accepted the second one before it could vanish.

Forty-two dollars. He was seven short of the wheel, so on Saturday he sold his old skateboard deck too, listing it low because three identical decks were already posted, and it sold within the hour for eighteen. He walked to the shop with sixty dollars folded in his pocket, past houses on the wider street where the affluent families lived, the ones with basketball hoops and trimmed hedges.

His mother patted his shoulder when he wheeled the repaired bike back into the garage. "See, patience," she said, and he let her reassure him even though patience wasn't quite what had done it. He had watched, adjusted, and found the number where everything moved. He rode a slow loop around the driveway as the sun went low, then called out through the open door, "Race you to the corner, Sonny!"

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
story:
Aiden sat on the porch steps of Grandpa's house with his notebook open, muttering family words in Mandarin until they stopped sounding like noise. His class had a project due Monday: describe your family and pets in full sentences, out loud, no English allowed. He could say "I have a dog" and even "my dog is old and slow," which was true about Biscuit. The trouble was the cousin part.

Grandpa set down two glasses of lemonade and peered at the notebook. "You write it ten times, you say it twenty times," he said. "That is how I learned English for my scholarship exam, sitting right on these steps."

"Did it work?"

"I am here, aren't I?" said Grandpa, and went back inside, quick and agile for someone who claimed his knees were eighty.

That evening a message arrived from Aiden's cousin Wenli, who lived two streets over and was helping him practice. Aiden read it on Grandpa's old tablet:

Aiden,
Good news: I checked with my mom, and I can come Saturday to hear your sentences. Bad news: I am bringing my brothers, so you have to say their part too. Fair warning, they are a handful. Also, you will need the right words, and I am not going to tell you which ones. Figure it out before I get there.
Wenli

Aiden groaned. Wenli had twin brothers, annoying and loud and exactly identical as far as Aiden could tell. How was he supposed to pick a word for people who were the same age?

He texted Mavis, who was in his class, but she only knew the words for older and younger sister, meimei and jiějie, because she had sisters. That gave him an idea, though. If Mandarin bothered to have two different sister words, it probably had two brother words too, and the same rule underneath them: older one word, younger another. He found the words in the back of his workbook: gēge and dìdi. So all he had to figure out was who was older.

Saturday morning, he asked the twins the moment they stomped onto the porch. "Which of you was born first?"

"I was," said Jin, shoving his brother toward the door. "By ten whole minutes."

"Then I have one gēge and one dìdi," Aiden said carefully, "because gēge means older brother, and dìdi means younger brother."

Wenli stopped halfway up the steps and stared. "Ten minutes counts," she admitted. "He never lets us forget it. Okay, now say all of it, the whole family, pets included."

Aiden took a breath, stood up straight, and said every sentence he had practiced twenty times on those steps. When he finished, the twins were actually quiet for once, and Wenli was grinning.

"That," she said, "was worth the trip. Say the dog part again."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Nicholas had worn his grandfather's watch for three days straight, and now Charles-Etienne had noticed. "You wear that every day now," Charles-Etienne said on the front step, tossing a bottle cap against the railing. "Since the funeral?"

"Since we cleaned out his apartment," Nicholas said. The watch was heavy and old, with a leather strap gone soft and dark. He had found it in the drawer next to the loose change, and he had put it on before he even decided to.

That night he couldn't sleep, so he lay still and monitored the ticking, which was faint but steady, like a tiny heartbeat under his wrist. A thought kept circling: maybe wearing it meant he was stuck. Kids at school talked about moving on. Auguste had said his aunt told him that after a while you had to let go and put things away. Nicholas pictured himself taking the watch off and putting it in a box, and something in his chest went tight.

He remembered the morning two summers ago when his grandfather taught him to fix the back gate. The screwdriver had slipped and Nicholas had sliced his thumb, and his grandfather had wrapped it in a handkerchief and said, "A project has casualties." Then they had finished the gate together anyway, and afterward they drank lemonade on the porch, the gate swinging open and shut on its new hinges. It had swung just right. His grandfather had made him open and close it six times to check.

The next morning Nicholas took the watch to Mr. Oyelaran next door, who was washing his car in the driveway. "Can I ask you something?" Nicholas said. "Is it bad if I keep wearing my grandpa's watch? Like I'm not moving on?"

Mr. Oyelaran turned off the hose. "There's a book called Continuing Bonds," he said. "Came out in 1996." He dried his hands slowly. "It says the opposite of what most people assume. Keeping a connection to someone who died, through memories, objects, traditions, that can be a healthy part of grieving."

"So I don't have to put it in a box?"

"Course not." Mr. Oyelaran picked up the sponge again. "You could even start something. A tradition. My family makes my mother's soup every November."

Nicholas rode his bike to Auguste's house and found Auguste and Charles-Etienne in the garage, arguing about a model rocket with an opaque plastic nose cone that had cracked in two. Nicholas set the watch carefully on the workbench, where his grandfather would have set it, sleeves rolled up, and picked up the glue.

"Fix the cone first, then the fins," he said. "That's how he'd do it."

Charles-Etienne handed him the glue. "This Saturday we could all go get lemonade. You know. On the porch."

"Same flavor," Nicholas said. "Two sugars."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
story:
The itch started during morning break, deep under the cast on Simon's left arm, in a spot he could not reach and could not even see. He pressed his palm against the plaster and rubbed, but the itch stayed where it was, stubborn as a fly. Around him the playground was loud with a football game, and the sun had already dried the sandpit into an arid little desert with footprints stamped across it.

"You're doing the face," said Jeanne, dropping onto the bench beside him. "The itchy face."

"It's worse today. Like something's crawling in there." Simon picked up his ruler from his bag, the flat wooden one with his name on the spine of it in marker, and turned it over in his good hand. He lined up the edge with the gap at the end of the cast.

Claire sat down fast. "Don't. My cousin did that with a pencil and it was a whole thing. The doctor said never slide anything in there, like pencils or sticks, because it can scrape the skin and wreck the lining of the cast too."

Simon lowered the ruler. He had not thought about the inside of the cast at all. He had been imagining his arm, but the cast was a layered thing, and the lining was part of it, hidden under the hard shell. If the pencil could damage something he could not see, then the inside was a place with rules of its own, like the far side of the moon.

"So how do you scratch an itch you can't get to?" he said.

Jeanne shrugged. "You just suffer, I think."

Simon looked at the ruler again. Flat, hard, wrong. But if the problem was that anything sliding in could scrape, then what he needed was something that did not scrape. Something with no edge at all. He got up, walked to the water fountain, and ran cold water over the outside of the cast until the plaster darkened in a patch right over the itchy spot. The cold seeped through, slow and dull, and the itch faded like a radio turned down.

He walked back to the bench holding his arm away from his shirt so the wet patch could dry. Claire leaned over and peered at it.

"Did that actually work?"

"Halfway," Simon said. He shook his arm gently, listening to the faint shift of the lining inside. "Want to time me? I bet I can make it to the bell without the ruler."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
Gabriella stood at the counter of the phone store, turning the small silver rectangle over in her hands while Mr. Traoré, the clerk, typed her mother's information into the computer. In her other hand she held a letter from her grandfather, who had sent money for her birthday with strict instructions that it be spent on a phone and nothing else.

"Read it again," whispered Megan, leaning over her shoulder. The letter was written in her grandfather's cramped handwriting, and it read: "Dear Gabriella. Congratulations on your first phone. When I was young, the first handheld cell phone call ever made was by a man named Martin Cooper, and that phone weighed about 1.1 kilograms, which is 2.5 pounds. My whole arm would have been tired after one call. Yours will weigh less than a sandwich. Use it to call me anyway. Love, Grandpa."

"Two and a half pounds," Gabriella said. "That's like a big bag of sugar." She tried to picture it. Her new phone felt like a thin chocolate bar. She picked up a display model of a chunky old-fashioned phone on the shelf, then a two-pound bag of rice at the store's demo station, holding one in each hand to compare. The rice was heavier. So Cooper's phone would have been heavier still. "That thing was a brick," she said. "A brick that could call people."

Mr. Traoré smiled and slid a protective case across the counter. "This one has a porous lining," he said. "If you spill juice on it, the fabric soaks it up instead of letting it reach the phone." Gabriella pressed her thumb into the soft material and watched it darken where her damp skin touched it. "That's the case I want," she said, and Megan nodded in agreement, because Megan had dropped her own phone into a puddle last spring.

Then came the hard part: the plan. Mr. Traoré showed them the pricing sheet, and Gabriella studied it, chewing her pencil. "If I want to know whether the family plan is better, I have to isolate the one thing that changes," she said slowly, covering the parts that stayed the same with her hand. "The data. Everything else is identical." She did the math twice, and when the second answer matched the first, she looked up. "The bigger plan saves ten dollars a month if we use it all."

Her mother signed the papers while Gabriella carefully folded the letter and tucked it into her back pocket. The phone was hers by the time they reached the door, warm in her hand, lighter than anyone in 1973 could have dreamed. She stopped on the sidewalk outside and typed her first message: "Hi Grandpa. It weighs nothing. Calling you tonight. G."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Olivia stared at her paper and the paper stared back, blank except for one dot in the middle. Ms. Koné had given the class until the end of lunch period to draw a street scene in one-point perspective, and the best drawings would hang in the hallway for the school open house tonight. Forty minutes. Olivia had already used up twelve of them panicking.

"The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals," Ms. Koné had said that morning, tapping the dot on her own example. "Draw your orthogonals first."

"Easy for her," Leighton whispered, sliding into the seat beside Olivia. He had already drawn a lopsided street that looked like it was melting. "Which lines are they, though? She never said."

"That's the whole problem," Olivia said. She looked at the dot again. Her street had to be full of stuff: buildings, curbs, roofs, maybe a shop with an awning. She wanted hers picked for the hallway so her grandfather, who was visiting for the open house, would see it.

Danae leaned over from the next table, chewing the end of her pencil. "I got it wrong," she said. "I drew the fronts of my buildings slanting. Ms. Koné circled them. Whatever an orthogonal is, it isn't that."

Olivia flipped back to Ms. Koné's example, which was still on the board. She put her finger near her own eye and traced along the drawing. The road edges went back to the dot. So did the curbs. She moved her finger up to the rooftops. The rooflines, too. Every line that ran back, away from her and toward the vanishing point, slanted toward that one dot. The fronts of the buildings, the parts facing her, stayed straight up and down.

"Road edges, curbs, rooflines," she said out loud. "They all go back to the dot."

"So the fronts stay flat," Leighton said, "and everything that runs away from you slants."

"That's it. That's the rule." Olivia grabbed her ruler before she could lose the idea. She drew the road edges first, thin and precise, both diving toward the dot. Then the curbs. Then the rooflines of a bakery and a bookstore. Danae erased her melting fronts and started over with her own ruler, tongue sticking out.

The lunch bell rang with its usual abrupt clang, and half the class groaned. Leighton's hand froze mid-line. "I'm not done."

"You've got ten minutes of recess," Danae said. "Ms. Koné said she'd take late finishers."

When Ms. Koné walked the rows, she stopped at Olivia's desk. "Where did you get the idea to start with the rooflines?"

"I followed your example backward, sort of," Olivia said. "Every line running back to the vanishing point, I drew it first."

Ms. Koné pinned the drawing to the hallway corkboard before the buses even left. Beside it, she hung a small note: "When I retire, my pension will buy me a real studio, and I will draw streets all day." Leighton read it and laughed so hard the teacher across the hall came out to dismiss him into the gym.
