Olivia stayed a moment longer, looking at her street, at the road narrowing toward its single distant dot, and her grandfather's footsteps came up behind her. "Which building is ours?" he asked.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and old sneakers, and Mr. Lau had already set out the ramp before the bell finished ringing. "Today you measure the speed of a rolling ball," he said, "and then you show me what it looks like on paper." Jayden picked up the stopwatch and turned it over in his hands. He wanted this to go right, because last week he had mixed up millimeters and centimeters on a measurement quiz, and Dev had made a point of announcing it to half the class. He was not going to give anyone a reason to ridicule him this time.

Shyla held the wooden ball at the top of the ramp. Teo crouched beside the floor with a meter stick laid out flat, a strip of masking tape marking every half meter. They had agreed on their ritual: Shyla released the ball, Teo called out each time it crossed a tape mark, and Jayden clicked the stopwatch and wrote the numbers down. On the first run the ball hit the stick and veered sideways, so they weighted the ramp with a folded towel and ran it again. The numbers came out cleaner this time: half a meter at one second, a full meter at two, one and a half at three.

"Two seconds, one meter," Jayden said, writing fast. "So it's rolling half a meter every second. That's the speed." He felt buoyant, almost light enough to float off the bleachers. All they had to do now was the graph.

Back in the classroom, Mr. Lau handed out grid paper and told them to plot their data. "One warning," he said. "I have seen groups draw this graph in a way that makes no sense at all, and they never figure out why. Good luck." Then he sat down at his desk and graded quizzes, which was his way of saying the rest was up to them.

Jayden drew his axes first. He liked the way a graph looked, with its neat lines and tidy corners. He put the seconds going up the side, one box at a time, and the distance going along the bottom. Then he plotted his points. Something was wrong. The points climbed up in fat, slow steps instead of forming the smooth diagonal line he had expected, and the whole shape looked like a staircase someone had squashed.

"Look at this," he said to Teo, turning the paper around. Teo squinted at it. Shyla leaned over Jayden's other shoulder. "It looks like the ball slowed way down at the end," she said, "but it didn't. It was the same speed the whole way. We measured that." Jayden tapped his pencil against the desk. Their numbers were fine. The ball had been fine. So the problem had to be in the drawing itself.

He looked at the axes again, then at the graph on the board from last month, the one about plant growth that Mr. Lau had left up for a week. On that graph, the days had run along the bottom and the height had gone up the side. "Time goes along the bottom," Jayden said slowly. "Distance goes up." He tore off a fresh sheet and drew it the other way, seconds along the horizontal axis and distance up the vertical one. The points fell into a straight diagonal line, climbing steadily from corner to corner.

"That's it," Shyla said. "That's what a steady speed looks like." Teo traced the line with his finger, from the empty corner up to the top of the page. Jayden carried the graph to Mr. Lau's desk and set it down without a word, and Mr. Lau looked at the axes first, before he looked at anything else.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
Arianna skated to the bench, legs burning, and watched Mavrick fly past her on the next drill. That was the third time this week he'd beaten her to the cone, and two weeks ago it hadn't even been close.

"He's on the ice every single day," Dave said, dropping beside her. "Even Sundays. My mom saw him here at seven in the morning, doing laps alone." Arianna stared at Mavrick carving tight turns at the far end. He trained more than anyone on the team, so he should be the fastest, but in Saturday's game he'd gotten slower and slower each period until the coach pulled him for a shift. Something about that didn't add up. She trained three days and rested the others, and she'd dropped half a second off her sprint since November.

That night she wrote it out in her notebook, incorporating every practice into a chart: who trained how many days, and their sprint times week by week. Mavrick: seven days a week, times getting worse. Her: four days a week, times getting better. Dave: five days, holding steady. She tapped the pencil against her chin. It was like trying to find where a laser beam was coming from without seeing the source; the effect was right there, but the cause was hidden. Maybe the ice time wasn't the thing that made you faster. Maybe the days between were.

On Sunday she found Mavrick alone at the rink café, poking at a plate of fries like a predatory hawk guarding food he was too tired to eat. "Can I show you something?" she asked, and slid the notebook across the table. He frowned at the chart, then at her. "So you're saying I should do less?" His voice had an edge. "I'm saying look at your numbers. Mine went down with rest days. Yours are going up without them."

Mr. Morales, who ran the skate rental counter, leaned over as he refilled the napkins. "My daughter swam competitively. Her coach always said the workout breaks you down and rest builds you back up." Arianna looked at Mavrick. "So the actual getting-better part happens when you're not training. Rest days are part of it. Try one full day off and see what your stopwatch says."

Mavrick took Sunday off, then Monday too, and grumbled the whole time like a bear denied a snack. At Wednesday practice he lined up beside Arianna for the sprint, jaw set. The whistle blew, and he pulled ahead by a full stride, then another, his skates biting the ice like they hadn't in weeks. He turned at the cone with a look of pure disbelief. "A whole stride," he panted, grinning. "I'm taking Sundays off forever. Maybe Saturdays too."

"Let's not get crazy," Arianna said, and pushed off toward the blue line.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
story:
Beatrice had promised her tent-mates a campfire demonstration, and now she had to deliver it without embarrassing herself. Tomorrow morning, back at school, each student in Ms. Qureshi's class had to teach a five-minute lesson from the trip, and Beatrice had drawn the question she dreaded most: why do we have seasons? Everyone said the answer out here, away from the library, and she had stubbornly, obstinately refused to look it up before leaving, because she wanted to figure it out herself. So far she had figured out nothing.

She sat on a log beside Ariella and Blaire, turning a flashlight in her hands. "I keep thinking it's distance," she said. "We're closer to the sun in summer, farther in winter. That has to be it."

"Then why is it summer in Australia when it's winter here?" Blaire asked. She was peeling the label off a water bottle in long strips. "My cousin lives there. She's swimming in December."

Beatrice frowned. If distance caused the seasons, the whole planet would warm up and cool down together, and December would be cold everywhere. "Okay," she said slowly. "So something else is different. Something that flips."

Ariella grabbed the flashlight and shone it straight down onto the dirt. A small, bright circle glowed on the ground, sharp-edged and intense. Then she tilted the flashlight, sweeping it sideways, and the circle stretched into a long, pale oval, so dim that the details of the soil came back into view underneath it.

"That's it," Beatrice said. She took the flashlight and held it upright again. "Look. Straight down, all that light lands in one little spot. Tilt it, and the same light gets spread across a bigger patch, so each bit of ground gets less of it." She swept the beam sideways again to check, and the oval faded exactly as before. "Same flashlight. Same light. It's just spread out."

"So the sun does that to the whole Earth?" Ariella asked.

Beatrice picked up a pinecone and held it level, then tipped it. She remembered the globe in Ms. Qureshi's room, tilted on its stand, and the way the teacher had spun it once without comment. The axis, she thought. The Earth leans, and the lean never changes direction. When our half of the planet leans toward the sun, the light comes down more straight, like the flashlight pointed down, concentrated on less ground, heating it more. That's summer. When we lean away, the light hits us slanted, spread thin. Winter. And half a year later we're on the other side, leaning the opposite way, while Australia leans the way we used to.

"Because of the tilt," she said out loud. "The Earth is tilted, and in summer the sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more. In winter it comes in at a slant."

"Show me again with the pinecone," Blaire said.

The next morning, Ms. Qureshi stood by the bus with her clipboard. When Beatrice's turn came, she held up the flashlight, aimed it at the patch of gravel by her boots, and said, "Somebody call out summer or winter, and I'll show you the whole year in ten seconds."

"Winter!" shouted Ariella, and Beatrice tilted the beam.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
story:
The lights died at 7:40, right in the middle of Gavin's homework, and the house went quiet in that strange way where even the refrigerator stops humming. His stomach growled almost immediately, which felt like bad timing. He opened the fridge door, and the little light did not come on. He peered into the cold dark, found nothing he wanted, and shut it. Five minutes later he opened it again, as if a plate of lasagna might have wandered in on its own.

"Stop doing that," his older brother said from the couch. "Every time you open it, you're letting the cold out. Ms. Mercado told me once that a fridge only keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, as long as the door stays closed the whole time." Gavin stood in the dark kitchen holding that thought like a flashlight. Four hours. One door, or a lot of little ones?

He decided to test it, in his own way. He grabbed his phone for its dying glow and walked next door to Ms. Mercado's house, where a lantern glowed in the front window and two familiar bikes were tipped over on the lawn. Paul and Rory were already inside, sitting on the kitchen floor arguing about the popsicles in Ms. Mercado's freezer.

"There are three grape and one orange," Paul said. "I called the orange one last week."

"You can't call a popsicle a week in advance," Rory said. "That's not a rule anywhere."

Gavin mediated the only way he knew how: he offered to flip a coin, and when both boys complained that a coin was unfair to grape lovers, he proposed rock, paper, scissors, best two out of three. Rory won the orange pop without a single argument after that, which proved something about human beings that Gavin filed away for later.

"I take it your power is out too," Ms. Mercado said, coming in with a tray of brittle peanut candy that snapped loudly when anyone bit it. Down the street, someone's generator thumped away like a giant piston, patient and steady. She set the tray between the boys and added, "Help yourselves, but we're keeping the fridge shut tonight."

"That's exactly my plan," Gavin said, and explained it. Decide what you want first, in your head, before touching the handle. Then open the door once, take it, and close it fast. He'd been opening his fridge every five minutes like a confused moth, and if he kept that up, the four hours of safe cold would leak away through his own fingers.

So they made a game of it. Paul announced he would want the leftover rice. Rory chose apple juice. Gavin, after serious deliberation, committed to turkey and mustard. When the power finally shuddered back on at 9:15, well inside the window, all three of them marched to the fridge, opened it exactly once, and retrieved their prizes in a single smooth raid.

Gavin bit into his sandwich at Ms. Mercado's counter and raised his juice-free hand in triumph. "One open," he said. "New house record."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The chicken thighs sat on the counter looking smug, and Nora did not trust them one bit. Tonight was Family Taste Night, when every seventh grader in Ms. Mehta's cooking class took home a full dinner, and Nora had promised her parents roasted chicken with lemon and garlic. The problem was that her group could not agree on anything.

"I say we pull it out now," said Daniyal, peering through the oven door. "It looks golden. Golden means done."

"That is so vague," said Leena. "Golden could mean anything. My hair is golden. Is my hair done?"

Ms. Mehta drifted past their station with a stack of dishes. "Interesting debate," she said, and kept walking, which was her way of telling them to figure it out themselves.

Nora pulled the pan out and stared at the chicken. It did look done. But last month her cousin had served chicken that looked perfect and pink near the bone, and the whole family remembered that dinner for a week. Looks were evidence, she decided, but not proof. There had to be a way to test what was actually happening inside, where her eyes could not go. Then she remembered the drawer of equipment by the sink, and dug through whisks and peelers until her hand closed on a slim metal probe with a digital screen. A thermometer. Of course. Heat was invisible, but it left a number behind, and numbers did not care about golden.

"Where do I even stick this thing?" she asked, holding it up.

"The thickest part," said Leena, reading off a laminated card by the sink. "That's where it cooks slowest. Push it in, don't touch the bone."

Nora slid the probe into the fattest part of the biggest thigh, the way you'd test the ripest peach in the bowl. The screen blinked, climbed, and settled: 158. She frowned at it. So close to done and yet somehow not, like arriving at a locked door with the right key still in your backpack. "Not yet," she announced. "Fifteen degrees short."

"Short of what?" asked Daniyal.

"Guidelines say 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 Celsius, in the thickest part," Nora read off the card. "Measured with a food thermometer. Not eyeballed. Thermometered."

"That's not a word," said Leena.

"It is now. I just generated it."

Back into the oven went the pan. Daniyal set the timer for five minutes and narrated the wait like a sports announcer, which mostly involved saying "the chicken is doing nothing" in an excited whisper. When the timer beeped, Nora tested the same thigh in the same spot. 166. The three of them cheered loudly enough that Ms. Mehta raised one eyebrow from across the room, and another group turned to see what all the noise was about.

"Okay, consensus time," said Leena. "All in favor of declaring this chicken done?" Three hands went up. "Motion passes. Daniyal, get the foil."

They wrapped the pan, and Nora carried it to the front table with both hands, walking the way you walk when you are carrying something important and slightly hot and your friend keeps shouting "Don't trip, chef!" behind you. Her dad would be waiting at the pickup door at five.

"Hey, Nora," Daniyal called after her. "Tell your family a thermometer saved their lives tonight."

"Tell them you generated dinner," Leena corrected, and Nora laughed so hard she had to stop and steady the pan, the steam rising past her face smelling of lemon and garlic.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Mr. Aquino's assignment sheet said one thing in bold: Explain why people moved west, using a primary source. Raphael read it twice on the bus and decided "primary source" was probably not a fancy water fountain.

"You're lucky," Mr. Aquino said at the museum, handing each of them a clipboard. "The archives let us look at copies of real settler diaries. Copies, so don't chew on them." Raphael took the folder labeled 1847-1849 and found a table near a glass case of butter churns, which smelled like old wood and lemon polish.

The diary belonged to a farmer named Ezra Pyle. The first entries were all dirt: rain, oxen, a bad tooth. Then the January 1848 page made Raphael sit up. "Word from California," it read. "Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill. Men drop their plows like the plows are on fire." Raphael frowned. He had written in his notebook, Farmers moved west for land. But Ezra Pyle already had land, and land was not making him run anywhere. Something else was pulling people, the way the earth pulls at a ball you toss, keeping it in orbit. Raphael tested it by reading forward. By June, Ezra had sold his farm. "I go not for soil," the June letter to his wife began, "but for gold. If I dig a fortune in one season, we are rich. If not, I dig again." So some of them wanted money, not farmland. That changed everything about his essay.

"It says he left a good farm," Moses said, reading over Raphael's shoulder. "That's the worst farming I ever heard of."

"He's not farming," Raphael said. "Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California, January 1848. It started the whole California Gold Rush. That's the hidden cause. Everybody thinks it's about soil, but half these people are chasing money."

Cayson crossed his arms. "Then why did my guy write forty pages about crop rotation?"

"Because people had different reasons," Raphael said. "That's the point. The gold thing is the pattern underneath." Cayson looked at his clipboard, looked at Raphael, and slowly crossed out his thesis sentence, which was the closest Cayson ever came to admitting anything.

In the last folder Raphael found an 1849 note from Ezra's wife, folded like a tiny intricate fan. "The neighbors call it gold fever," she had written. "Three more wagons left Tuesday. Mrs. Hart sold her piano to buy a mule. I have planted the beans alone and I do not complain, though I would like the piano back." Raphael copied it word for word, then underlined gold fever twice. Somewhere out there, Mrs. Hart was probably still regretting the mule.

On the ride home, Mr. Aquino collected their notes. He read Raphael's page, raised one eyebrow, and said, "A jury of historians would accept this."

"Even Cayson's half?" Raphael asked.

"Even Cayson's half," Mr. Aquino said, and handed it back.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
story:
Gabriella stood at the edge of the gym with the other Owls, waiting for Mr. Pereira to set up the relay cones. Nobody was looking at the cones. Everyone was looking at Van, who had just tripped over the mat and knocked the water bottle bucket sideways.

"Somebody can't even walk and carry a bottle at the same time," Devon sneered, and a few kids laughed. Van's ears went red. The gym had at least fifteen kids in it, plus two parents on the bleachers, and every single one of them was watching. Nobody said anything. Gabriella waited for one of the older kids to speak up, and then she waited for one of the parents, and then the moment stretched out so long that Devon found something else to say.

"Maybe we should put Van in a special category," Devon went on. "Like, the falling-down team."

Gabriella's stomach hurt. She wanted to help, but she had learned the hard way in fourth grade that yelling at a bully just gave the audience a better show. Yelling made everything louder. So she tried the opposite, and kept her voice as flat as if she were asking about homework. "Van, Mr. Pereira wants you for the relay." He didn't, but Van grabbed a bottle and came over fast, and the group scattered toward the cones.

"He didn't say that," Van whispered, hugging the bottle.

"I know." Gabriella watched Devon wander off. "Did you notice nobody helped you? Fifteen people watching." It bothered her all through the passing drills. Fifteen people, and it was like each one figured somebody else would step in. She thought about it while she ran, because it felt like a rule, something invisible but real, like the way a whole flock of birds turns at once.

After practice, her older sister was waiting in the car, and Gabriella told her about it on the drive home. "Oh," her sister said, tapping the wheel. "That's called the bystander effect. People are less likely to help when a bunch of others are watching, because everyone assumes someone else will act."

"That's exactly what it felt like," Gabriella said. "Like a math problem. If fifteen people all think someone else will move, then the answer is zero."

At the next practice, Devon started in on Van's sneakers, the ones with the duct tape on the toe. Gabriella didn't shout. She just walked over, stood next to Van, and said, in her flattest, most boring voice, "They're fine. Are we doing relay first or sprints?" Francesca drifted over too, and then a boy from the other end of the line, and after a second the whole group was arguing about sprints, which was not interesting to tease anyone about. Devon's face implied he'd lost his audience, and he dropped it.

Later, while they were packing up, Mr. Pereira held up the team banner, the one with the owl on it. "Who wants to carry this at the meet Saturday? The owl is our mascot, you know. Nocturnal bird. Hunts in the dark, sees everything."

"I'll carry it," Van said, so quietly it almost got lost in the zipper of the ball bag.

"Good," said Gabriella, and handed Van the pole.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
story:
The flyer on Grandpa's kitchen table looked too good to be true. "Turn $200 into $270 in five years," it said in bold letters, "with three percent simple interest." Bentley had come to Grandpa's house for the weekend with his math homework, and this flyer was the homework, sort of. Ms. Mori had torn it off a bank window and handed it to the whole class. "Find out if the bank is telling the truth," she'd said. "Or find out if it's hiding something."

Bentley texted Mayson, who was doing the same assignment across town. "Bank says $200 becomes $270. That's $70 interest. Something feels off." Mayson replied with a shrug emoji, which was no help at all. McKinley sent a voice message: "Just use the formula, dude. The simple interest formula is I equals P times r times t. Interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years." Bentley copied it onto a napkin. Two hundred dollars was the principal. Three percent, or 0.03, was the rate. Five years was the time. He multiplied: 200 times 0.03 equals 6, and 6 times 5 equals 30.

Thirty dollars. Not seventy. He checked it twice, then a third time with the calculator on his phone, and the number stared back at him, stubborn and small. The bank had promised $70. Either the flyer was wrong, or he was, and one of those options made his stomach tighten. "Grandpa," he called, "do you have graph paper?" He wanted to see it laid out properly, year by year, because there was one thing nagging him. If the money earned $6 the first year, did the second year's $6 land on the original $200, or on $206? The flyer said simple. Simple, he decided, had to mean the first way.

In the drawer under the phone charger, he found a letter Grandpa had saved from his own father, written decades ago. "Dear Son," it read, "the credit union man came by with papers today. I asked him three times to emphasize the word simple in the contract. Simple means the interest never earns interest. Watch for that word, and watch for people who say it quietly." Bentley read the line twice, a chill walking up his arms.

So the pattern held. Simple meant $30, flat and inevitable, no matter how many years stacked up. He texted Mayson one more time: "It's a trick. $30 is honest. The $70 must be compound, where the interest earns interest too. They put the big number in bold so nobody asks which one it is." He sat back and looked at his napkin, covered now with careful arithmetic, and slid it across the table toward Grandpa. "The bank's hiding something," Bentley said, tapping the flyer. "Read the fine print. Which kind of interest is it really?"

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
story:
Jeremy typed his first line of real Python and hit enter so fast the keyboard rattled. The computer lab hummed around him, twenty machines all awake at once, and Ms. Dela Cruz had promised that anyone who finished the practice problem could try a challenge problem instead. The practice problem was his: write a program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime.

"Watch this," he said to Simeon, who leaned over from the next seat. Jeremy ran the program, typed 7, and the screen printed "prime." He typed 9, and it printed "not prime," because his loop caught 3 dividing into it. He pumped both fists in the air.

Simeon wasn't even looking. He had a crumpled printout on his desk, a page he'd torn from a library book about numbers, and his plan was bigger. "If your program works," he said, "we feed it bigger and bigger numbers. I'm going to find the largest prime number. They'll put my name in the paper."

"Coach says my brother has an allergy to losing," Simeon added, "so it runs in the family." He smoothed the page flat and squinted at it. Then his face fell. "Wait. Listen to this." He read aloud in a slow voice, as if the words might change if he rushed them. "Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers."

Jeremy read the sentence himself, twice. "So there's no largest one," he said. "There can't be. Whatever you find, there's always another one past it." It felt strange and great at the same time, like hearing that the hallway went on forever past the gym doors. He couldn't see the endless primes, but the rule was sitting right there on the page, proved before anyone had computers at all.

While Simeon groaned about his lost newspaper headline, a message popped up on the shared class forum from Carina, who was home sick and following the lesson online. "Dear lab people," she wrote. "I extracted the challenge problem from the folder Ms. Dela Cruz posted, and it says to test our programs on the number 2. Mine says 2 is not prime and I think that's wrong. Also tell Simeon the keyboard is not a drum."

Simeon laughed so hard Ms. Dela Cruz looked over, one eyebrow raised. Jeremy turned back to his screen. His loop started dividing at 2 and never let 2 divide into itself, so he had made the same mistake Carina had. He fixed the first check, saved the file, and typed 2 into the input box. The cursor blinked at him, waiting, and his finger hovered above the enter key. "Two," he whispered. "Show me prime."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: A heading is a block element that stretches across the full width of its container, which is why text-align: center puts its text in the middle of the page.
story:
Aubrey had one goal for Saturday morning at the public library: get the big purple heading on her web page to sit in the middle of the screen. It sat stubbornly on the left, like it had paid rent there. She had already saved her file about forty times, and it still hadn't moved. Her friend Grey slid into the chair beside her and peered at the screen.

"Maybe the middle isn't where you think it is," Grey said. "Where is the middle, anyway?" Aubrey frowned at the heading. She knew that a heading was a block element that stretched across the full width of its container. That was the piece she kept turning over. If the heading already went all the way across, then the text inside it could be pushed to the centre of that whole width. She typed a new line into her CSS: text-align: center. She saved, then hit refresh. The purple words glided to the middle of the page.

"Okay, that was satisfying," Aubrey said, and Grey laughed so loudly that Ms. Ahmadi, the librarian, raised one eyebrow from behind the front desk. Aubrey lowered her voice. "I think I get it now. The heading was always stretching across the whole page. I just couldn't see that part. The words were hiding on the left of it." To test the idea, she gave the heading a temporary background colour. A solid purple band appeared, reaching from one edge of the page to the other. Grey pointed at it. "It's a full-width banner. The whole time."

Their classmate Reet arrived late, breathless, carrying a library book about coding that she'd been renewing for weeks. "Did you fix it?" she whispered. Aubrey changed the background back to normal and demonstrated the trick again, typing the CSS line slowly so Reet could watch the heading slide into place. Reet tried it on her own laptop and got it on the first try, which felt almost unfair, but Aubrey found she felt more proud than anything else. A week ago she'd been nursing a small resentment toward computers for making no sense. Now they seemed like puzzles that would actually crack, given enough Saturday mornings.

"This is permanent now," Aubrey said. "I'm never forgetting text-align: center." Grey snorted. "You'll forget everything else, though." Probably true, Aubrey thought, but that was fine, because the library was open every day and Ms. Ahmadi never seemed to mind the whispers. Aubrey started a brand new page, just for practice, and typed the first heading. She centered it immediately, then added a second one below it, grinning as the words landed right where she wanted them.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Sarah had blown her nose eleven times before lunch, and her nose still felt blocked, packed like a sock in a drainpipe. She sat on the couch with a box of tissues, a bowl of soup gone cold, and her phone. She was home with the flu, and she had decided that if she had to be miserable, she could at least be miserable like a scientist.

She texted Harlee: "If my nose is full of mucus, why does nothing come out when I blow it?" Harlee replied with a shrug emoji and then, three minutes later, "weird." Sarah frowned at the screen. Blowing harder did nothing. Blowing gently did nothing. She got one crumpled tissue and rolled it into a plug, then held it near her nostril and breathed out. The tissue barely fluttered, which meant almost no air was moving. If the passage were full of mucus, some of it should come out. Something else had to be blocking the way, something she couldn't see directly. She would have to test an idea.

The idea came from a flashback. Last winter, her friend Fraser, who was her mentor in the school science club because he was a year older and knew everything about bugs, had sat beside her at the sink during a meeting. He had run the hot tap, draped a towel over his head, and breathed the steam. "When my nose blocks up," he had said, "steam shrinks the swelling. My gran taught me." Sarah had thought it was nonsense then. Now she wondered what swelling he meant, since there was nothing in her nose to swell as far as she could tell, unless the blocking was not mucus at all but the tissue of the nose itself, puffed up from the inside like an inflamed blister. That would explain why blowing gave no relief. Steam might bring the swelling down, at least an approximate amount, enough to breathe.

She went to the kitchen and ran the hot tap. She draped a dish towel over her head and leaned into the rising mist. Her glasses fogged and she took them off. After a minute her right nostril opened with a small pop of air, and she breathed through it, loud and delighted, like someone surfacing. The left one stayed stubborn. She retrieved the rolled tissue and held it under the open nostril; it fluttered strongly now. So the blockage could shrink without anything being blown out. It wasn't a buildup. It was the lining itself, inflamed, with swollen vessels inside it.

"Sarah, why is the kettle on and you're under a towel?" Her mother stood in the doorway with a bag of cough drops.

"Experiment," Sarah said, surfacing. "My nose isn't plugged with mucus. It's swollen from the inside. Steam helps the swelling go down. Fraser showed me last year."

Her mother set the bag down. "Your grandmother used to say the same thing, and I told her it was mucus. I've been saying that for thirty years." She picked up Sarah's phone from the counter and looked at the search screen, then at her daughter. "You checked this?"

Sarah peeled back the towel. "Steam test, tissue test, and it's on the medical site too. Swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue, not mucus buildup."

Her mother put the kettle on properly, took two mugs from the cupboard, and said, "Then make room under that towel."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
story:
Chloe had been begging to learn her grandmother's pasta sauce for months, and today was finally the day. Ainsley's kitchen smelled like garlic and possibility, and Joseph was already there setting out three cutting boards like this was a competition.

"First lesson is the onion," Ainsley said, handing Chloe a knife. "Claw grip. Curl your fingertips under so the knife rides your knuckles. You'd have to try pretty hard to cut yourself."

Chloe curled her fingers and pressed down on the onion. The knife squashed instead of slicing, and it skated sideways, off the onion and onto the board. She tried again, pushing harder, and this time the blade slipped off the papery skin and nearly went off the cutting board entirely.

"Whoa," Joseph said. "Maybe you're pressing too hard?"

"I'm barely pressing at all," Chloe lied, because she was pressing plenty. She looked at the knife. It was the dullest thing in the room, duller than Joseph's pencil case, maybe duller than Tuesday. That had to be the problem. A knife this blunt couldn't bite into anything; it just slid around until it found somewhere to go, and somewhere to go meant her fingers. "Ainsley, got a sharper knife? I think this one's the whole problem."

Ainsley rummaged in the drawer and swapped in a different knife, one that caught the light along its edge. Chloe set it on the onion, barely leaned on it, and the blade sank clean through with almost no pressure. She did it again. And again. It felt like a magic trick, except it was obviously just the sharp knife doing the work instead of her arm. "Did you see that? It needs way less pushing, so it doesn't go flying off the food. I'm never using a dull knife again. Dull knives are the dangerous ones, not sharp ones."

"That actually makes sense," Joseph said slowly, like a person diagnosing why his bike kept squeaking after he'd oiled everything except the one part that mattered.

They diced the onions, crushed the canned tomatoes with their hands, which was the best part, and let the sauce bubble while Mr. Warsame, Ainsley's neighbour, wandered in for his usual Saturday visit. He raised his eyebrows at the pot.

"You three made that from scratch? I thought you'd order pizza like every kid since the recession ruined everyone's confidence in the kitchen."

"We're not that gullible," Joseph said. "Store sauce is just sugar and sad. Try this."

Mr. Warsame accepted a spoonful, chewed, and closed his eyes like he was composing a compliment. Chloe ladled more sauce over the pot of pasta Ainsley was draining, steam billowing up between them.

"Next week," Chloe announced, "lasagna. And I'm bringing my own knife."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet.
story:
The kitten had been at the shelter for eleven days, and Easton had visited on nine of them, which felt like a reasonable amount of evidence that he was serious. Mr. Saleh, who ran the front desk, finally slid the paperwork across. "Her name's on the card as Pumpkin, but you can negotiate that with her, not me."

"I'm keeping it," Easton said, picking up the carrier. Pumpkin pressed her face to the mesh and sneezed.

At home, his mother read the feeding sheet twice. "We're vegetarians," she said slowly. "So she can just eat what we eat, right? Beans, rice, eggs?"

Easton was hesitant to argue, since his mother had written a school report on plant-based protein. But something snagged in his mind. On his nine visits, he had watched the shelter cats at their leisure, sprawled in the sun on the windowsill, and he had never once seen any of them touch the bowl of kibble that smelled like fish. Every single cat chose the meaty one. That was a pattern, and patterns usually meant something.

"Give me tonight," he said. "I want to test it."

He set two saucers on the kitchen floor: one with rice and mashed lentils, one with a small can of chicken. Pumpkin circled both, sniffed the lentils, and walked away from them like they were a homework assignment. Then she inhaled the chicken in ninety seconds flat. Easton wrote it down. He tried again at breakfast with eggs and cheese, and she ate a little, but she left most of it and sat by the cupboard where the chicken can had been, staring at it with enormous direct eyes. Two trials, same result.

At school he told Allie, who frowned. "Maybe she just dislikes lentils. I dislike lentils."

"That's the thing, though." Easton showed her the page in the shelter's care packet that he'd found shoved in the bottom of the carrier. Allie read it out loud. "Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet."

"What's an obligate carnivore?"

"Basically a carnivore that has no choice about it." He tapped the page. "So it's not that Pumpkin is picky. It's that her whole body is built that way. That's the hidden cause. She wasn't turning up her nose at Mom's cooking."

His mother read the packet that evening and nodded. "Then we shop for her, not for us." Camden came along to the pet store, where they compared labels and argued about whether the one shaped like tiny fish was superior to the one shaped like tiny stars. Easton carried the bag home with the proud, careful grip of someone transporting treasure.

That night Pumpkin ate her dinner in the laundry room, crunching so loudly they could hear it from the kitchen. When she finished, she hopped onto Easton's bed, kneaded the blanket twice, and fell asleep against his elbow. He stayed very still, one arm going numb, and didn't move until morning.

"Best negotiation I ever lost," he whispered.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
story:
On his fourth day home from school with the flu, Justin decided he had waited long enough. His plan was simple: convince his mom to take him to the pharmacy, ask the pharmacist for antibiotics, and be back at school by Friday, where a five-on-five soccer game against Alexandre's class was scheduled. He rehearsed his argument all the way there, curled in the passenger seat while she talked on the phone about their mortgage, something about payments and winter and "we'll interpret the letter when it comes."

At the pharmacy, Justin marched up to the counter while his mom hunted for tissues. "I need antibiotics," he announced. "For the flu. I have a game on Friday."

The pharmacist, a woman with glasses pushed up into her hair, looked up from a stack of boxes. "Antibiotics kill bacteria," she said. "They have no effect on viruses. A cold or the flu is a virus, so they won't help cure it." She slid a box of flu remedies toward him. "Fluids, rest, and time. That's the whole arsenal."

Justin stood there, feeling the plan collapse in an abrupt and total way, like a snow fort in March. Bacteria and viruses were two different things, then, and medicine only fought one of them. That was why he'd gotten better from his ear infection last spring with those pink pills, but not from this. He turned the idea over while the pharmacist rang up his mom's tissues. So the pills weren't weak, exactly. They were just aimed at a different target, like bringing a hockey stick to a soccer game.

At school on Monday, still a little sniffly but cleared by his mom, he found Alexandre by the lockers. "You missed a great game," Alexandre said. "We lost anyway. Lilly scored four goals on us."

"I figured something out while I was sick," Justin said. He told him about bacteria and viruses, and how antibiotics only worked on one of the two. Alexandre squinted. "So if I get the flu, medicine can't fix it?"

"Not that kind. You just have to wait it out."

"That's terrible news," Alexandre said. "Waiting is my worst subject." He slammed his locker shut. "Come on, Lilly's rebounding for whoever shows up at the net after school."
